The Case for Protecting Fair Competition in Women's Sports

Introduction

The question of eligibility criteria in women's sports divisions is one of the most contentious issues in contemporary athletics. While compassion and inclusion are important social values, the fundamental purpose of sex-segregated sports categories demands serious examination. Women's sports divisions exist precisely because biological sex differences create meaningful competitive disparities. Allowing transgender women to compete in women's categories, regardless of transition status, undermines the very rationale for having women's sports at all. A categorical policy preserving women's sports for biological females is the most defensible approach to maintaining competitive fairness.

The Biological Foundation of Sex-Segregated Sport

Sports are not divided by gender identity — they are divided by sex, and for good reason. The biological differences between male and female development are not minor or cosmetic. They are systemic, measurable, and competitively significant.

Testosterone and Male Puberty

Male puberty, driven by vastly higher testosterone levels sustained over years, produces a cascade of physiological changes that confer athletic advantages:

  • Skeletal structure: Males develop broader shoulders, longer limbs relative to torso, larger hands and feet, wider bone frames, and different hip-to-shoulder ratios. These structural differences affect leverage, reach, stride length, and mechanical efficiency in virtually every sport.

  • Cardiovascular capacity: Males develop larger hearts (approximately 20-30% greater cardiac output), greater lung volume and capacity, and higher hemoglobin concentrations, resulting in superior oxygen delivery to working muscles.

  • Muscle mass and composition: Males carry approximately 40-60% greater muscle mass, particularly in the upper body. Male muscle fibers tend to be larger, and the ratio of lean mass to body fat is substantially different.

  • Height: The average male is approximately five inches taller than the average female, a factor that is decisive in sports like basketball, volleyball, and swimming.

These are not marginal differences. The performance gap between elite male and elite female athletes is approximately 10-15% across most sports, and substantially larger in events emphasizing upper body strength and explosive power. To put this in perspective, this gap is so large that thousands of high school boys routinely surpass the times, distances, and records of elite professional women.

The Persistence of Advantage After Transition

The central scientific question is whether hormone therapy eliminates these advantages. The evidence strongly suggests it does not — at least not fully, and perhaps not even substantially in the areas that matter most.

A landmark 2020 study published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine by Roberts et al. examined the fitness test results of transgender servicemembers in the U.S. Air Force. After two years of feminizing hormone therapy, transgender women still maintained a 9% advantage in running speed over cisgender women and retained significant advantages in push-up performance. Critically, these advantages persisted even after testosterone had been suppressed to female-typical levels for extended periods.

Research by Timothy Roberts and subsequent work by Emma N. Hilton and Tommy R. Lundberg, published in Sports Medicine (2021), found that:

  • Lean body mass decreased by only approximately 5% after two years of hormone therapy, leaving transgender women with substantially greater muscle mass than biological females.
  • Bone density and skeletal structure do not meaningfully change with hormone therapy in adults.
  • Lung capacity, heart size, and cardiovascular infrastructure remain essentially male.
  • Height, limb length, hand size, and skeletal frame are permanent.

The International Olympic Committee itself, after decades of attempting to craft inclusive policies, essentially acknowledged in its 2021 framework that no testosterone threshold or suppression period has been scientifically validated as eliminating male advantage. This was, in effect, an admission that the prior policy of requiring two years of testosterone suppression below 10 nmol/L was not grounded in solid evidence of fairness.

Dr. Ross Tucker, a prominent sports scientist, has summarized the evidence plainly: hormone therapy reduces but does not eliminate the physiological advantages conferred by male puberty. The retained advantages are not trivial — they are precisely the advantages that justify sex-segregated competition in the first place.

The Purpose and History of Women's Sports

Women's sports divisions were not created on the basis of gender identity. They were created because without a protected category, biological females would be effectively excluded from competitive athletics at the elite level.

Title IX in the United States, passed in 1972, was specifically designed to ensure that biological females had equal opportunities to participate in athletics. The decades since have seen remarkable growth in women's sports — from the explosion of women's collegiate athletics to the growing prominence of professional women's leagues and the expanding visibility of women in the Olympic Games.

This progress was built on one foundational premise: that women deserve a competitive space where they can compete against athletes of comparable biological capacity. Removing the sex-based criterion for entry into that space effectively demolishes the foundation.

Consider the implications. If we accept that any person who identifies as a woman should be eligible for women's competition regardless of biology, then women's sports no longer function as a protected category for biological females. The category becomes, in principle, open to any male-bodied individual who identifies as female. The logical endpoint is that women's sports would increasingly be populated by athletes who went through male puberty, and biological females — the very people the category was created to protect — would find themselves displaced.

This is not a hypothetical concern. Cases have already emerged across multiple sports and competitive levels.

Real-World Cases Illustrating the Problem

Lia Thomas — A swimmer who competed for three seasons on the University of Pennsylvania men's team, ranking in the mid-400s nationally, transitioned and subsequently won the NCAA Division I women's 500-yard freestyle championship in 2022. Thomas went from being an unremarkable male swimmer to a national champion in women's competition. Teammates and competitors — many of whom were afraid to speak publicly for fear of social repercussions — expressed frustration that years of their own training and sacrifice were rendered meaningless by competing against someone who had undergone male puberty.

Laurel Hubbard — A New Zealand weightlifter who competed in men's weightlifting before transitioning and went on to qualify for the 2020 Tokyo Olympics in women's weightlifting at age 43, an age when most weightlifters are well past their prime. While Hubbard did not medal in Tokyo, the qualification itself — at an advanced competitive age — illustrated the residual advantages of a male-developed musculoskeletal system.

CeCé Telfer — Won the NCAA Division II women's 400-meter hurdles championship in 2019 after previously competing on the men's team. Telfer went from an unranked male athlete to a national champion in women's competition.

Various high school cases — Multiple instances have emerged of transgender athletes dominating high school girls' competitions in track and field, with biological girls losing scholarship opportunities and championship titles.

In each of these cases, the pattern is consistent: athletes who were unremarkable or average in men's competition became dominant or highly competitive in women's competition after transition. This pattern is exactly what the physiological evidence predicts and is precisely the outcome that a protected women's category is designed to prevent.

The Fairness Argument

Sports are defined by rules that constrain competition to make it meaningful. Weight classes exist in boxing and wrestling because competing without them would be dangerous and unfair. Age divisions exist in youth sports because developmental differences at various ages make open competition inequitable. Paralympic classifications exist because different disabilities affect athletic capacity differently.

Sex-segregated competition exists for the same fundamental reason: without it, a protected space for biological females to compete would not exist. Every argument for sex-segregated sport is, at its foundation, a biological argument. If biology didn't matter, there would be no reason to separate men's and women's competition.

Those who argue for the inclusion of transgender women in women's sport must contend with an uncomfortable logical consequence: if the retained biological advantages don't matter, then the justification for women's sports as a separate category collapses entirely. You cannot simultaneously argue that biological sex differences justify a protected women's category and that those same biological differences are irrelevant when the athlete identifies as a woman.

Fairness in sport is not merely about subjective feelings or social belonging — it is about the conditions of competition. An athlete may sincerely identify as a woman, may live as a woman in every social respect, and may deserve dignity and acceptance in all domains of life. But competitive sport is one of the very few arenas where biological sex has direct, measurable, and consequential effects on outcomes. Pretending otherwise does not serve fairness — it abandons it.

Addressing Counterarguments

"Not all transgender women are dominant."

This is true but irrelevant to the principle. Not every heavyweight boxer who fights a lightweight would win — but we still maintain weight classes because the structural advantage makes competition systematically unfair. The question is not whether every transgender woman will win, but whether the category retains its integrity as a fair competition among biological females. A policy must be based on the systematic reality, not individual anecdotes.

"Testosterone suppression eliminates the advantage."

As detailed above, the scientific evidence does not support this claim. Suppressing testosterone reduces some advantages but leaves intact many of the most consequential ones: skeletal structure, height, lung capacity, cardiovascular infrastructure, and a significant portion of muscle mass. The advantages that remain are precisely the kind that determine outcomes in athletic competition.

"Excluding transgender women is discriminatory."

Women's sports are, by definition, exclusionary — they exclude males in order to provide fair competition for females. This exclusion is not based on animus; it is based on a recognition that biology matters in athletic competition. The eligibility criterion for women's sports has always been biological sex, not gender identity. Maintaining that criterion is not discrimination against transgender people any more than weight classes discriminate against heavier athletes. It is a classification system designed to ensure fair competition.

Moreover, inclusion of transgender women in women's sport creates its own form of discrimination — against biological females who lose competitive opportunities, scholarships, roster spots, championships, and records to athletes with male-derived physical advantages.

"There are so few transgender athletes that it doesn't really matter."

Fairness is a principle, not a numbers game. If even one biological female loses a championship or scholarship to a competitor with male-derived advantages, that is an injustice. And as social acceptance of transgender identities grows — which is a positive social development — the number of transgender athletes will likely increase, making this issue more consequential over time, not less.

"We should find a middle ground, like testosterone thresholds."

The IOC and multiple sporting bodies have spent decades attempting to find such a middle ground. Testosterone thresholds of 10 nmol/L, then 5 nmol/L, and various time requirements have been tried. None have been scientifically validated as sufficient to eliminate male advantage. The 2021 IOC framework essentially conceded this point by moving away from universal standards and deferring to individual federations. This has produced a patchwork of inconsistent rules and ongoing controversy. A clear, categorical policy based on biological sex is more transparent, more consistent, and more defensible than an endlessly contested threshold system that satisfies neither side and cannot be grounded in definitive science.

The Moral Dimension: Who Are We Protecting?

At the heart of this debate is a question of priorities. On one side, there are transgender women who wish to compete in the category that aligns with their gender identity — a desire that is understandable and comes from a genuine place. On the other side, there are millions of biological females who depend on the integrity of women's sports categories for their opportunity to compete fairly.

Women fought for decades to build the opportunities that exist today. Female athletes train with extraordinary dedication, sacrifice enormously, and compete at the highest levels their biology allows. They deserve a competitive space that is genuinely theirs — not one that is compromised by the inclusion of athletes whose physiology was shaped by male puberty.

This is not about questioning anyone's identity or denying anyone's humanity. It is about recognizing that competitive sport operates on biological realities, and that fairness for the many cannot be sacrificed for the inclusion of the few.

Transgender individuals deserve respect, acceptance, and opportunities to participate in sport. But those opportunities must be structured in ways that do not compromise the fairness of competition for biological females. Potential alternatives — including open categories, transgender-specific divisions, or mixed-gender formats — deserve exploration. What does not deserve acceptance is a policy that effectively tells biological girls and women that their competitive opportunities are secondary to the inclusion preferences of male-bodied athletes.

Conclusion

The case for a categorical policy preserving women's sports for biological females is grounded in biology, supported by evidence, consistent with the historical purpose of sex-segregated sport, and motivated by a commitment to fairness for female athletes.

Male puberty confers profound and enduring physiological advantages that hormone therapy does not eliminate. These advantages are not theoretical — they manifest in real competition, producing real losses for real female athletes. The integrity of women's sport depends on maintaining sex-based eligibility criteria, just as it always has.

Compassion and fairness are not mutually exclusive. We can affirm the dignity of transgender individuals while also protecting the competitive opportunities that generations of women fought to secure. But we cannot protect those opportunities if we abandon the biological basis on which they rest.

A clear, categorical rule — women's sports for biological females — is the fairest, most transparent, and most defensible policy. It protects the athletes who have the most to lose and preserves the meaning of the category that was created for them. It is the right policy — not because it is easy, but because fairness demands it.
